newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks end week lower ahead of U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks end week lower ahead of U.S. data.

text.p: Asia stocks ended lower after taking their cue from a downturn in the London and New York markets overnight as traders prepared for the release of key U.S. employment data due later on Friday.
The mood was particularly evident in Hong Kong, where the key Hang Seng index slipped after winning a hard fought battle to top the key 12,000 level on Thursday.
"We have moved up very strongly, and any consolidation would be healthy to provide a base for a trading range," said Miles Remington, sales trader at Crosby Securities.
The Hang Seng Index, which advanced for seven straight days and tacked on 225 points this week alone, ended off 109.05 points, or 0.91 percent, lower at 11,905.51.
In London, the FTSE-100 eased on Thursday to 4,000 points to end 15.1 points, or 0.04 percent, lower after touching 4,024.3.
It continued to slide early Friday and by 0939 GMT, the index was down 13.5 points at 3,986.5.
Similarly, a mild bout of profit-taking snapped the Dow Jones Industrial Average's four-day rally on Thursday, leaving the Dow off 1.12 at 5,932.85.

The Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged for now and other recent economic data have taken some of the usual intense focus off the September figures, although that could change if they fall wide of economists' forecasts.
Economists in New York look for the creation of 166,000 new jobs in September, down from 250,000 in August.
Tokyo shares ended lower ahead of the U.S. employment figures and concern over Japan's October 20 general election.
The key Nikkei 225-share average ended down 183.47 points or 0.86 percent at 21,148.03.
Shares in the Philippines made a dramatic recovery before the close after a broker stepped in and bought up stock in blue chip Ayala Land, a victim of a shakeout in the property sector.
After being down more than a point, the Manila stock index closed 0.88 points, or 0.03 percent, higher at 3,131.14 points.
In Seoul, shares were lower, pressured by mounting tensions on the Korean peninsula after Northe Korea threatened to retaliate over a submarine incident.
The composite index dropped 17.58 points or 2.21 percent to close at 776.43.
Thai stocks dropped 2.11 percent as heavy selling of bank and finance stocks pushed the market down 21.65 points to a close of 1,004.89.
Concern over the economy and political unrest that has led to a call for elections in November has pressured Thai stocks in recent weeks.

In Singapore, where the focus shifted to Malaysian stocks traded over the counter, the Straits Times Index ended down 1.90 points or 0.09 percent at 2,148.86. The Kuala Lumpur composite index closed up 2.46 points or 0.21 percent at 1,150.18.
Taiwan proved the exception to most of Asia, with its key index adding 4.63 points, or 0.07 percent, to reach a new 1996 closing high of 6,616.21.
Pakistan stocks dropped below 1,400 amid concern over news the country has not made headway in a bid to unfreeze its standby loan from the International Monetary Fund.

The Karachi 100-share index, after 60 minutes of trade, was down 16.09 points, or 1.14 percent, at 1,394.68 in the first Friday trading session in almost 20 years. The Karachi market has switched from a Friday/Saturday weekend to a Saturday/Sunday weekend to be in touch with overseas markets.

In Tokyo, the dollar was firmer in late trade but range-bound, having spent the day moving from 111.41 to 111.68 yen as the market waited for September U.S. jobs data, due out at 1230 GMT today. At 1045 GMT, the dollar traded at 111.45/1.55 yen and 1.5305/10 marks.
SIMEX Brent futures prices were higher in late trading, extending overnight gains seen in London. November last traded at $23.78 per barrel, up four cents from London's Thursday settlement of $23.74.
Hong Kong gold bullion ended at US$380.10/60 an ounce against New York's US$380.10/50 close on Thursday.
